summary: This informational RFC describes Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE), which uses identity-based encryption so a sender can pass a shared secret to a receiver. The receiver's identity serves as the public key. It is published for information rather than as a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally to send a secret you first need the receiver's special lock. With this method, the receiver's name works as the lock, so you can send a secret to anyone whose name you know.

subtitle: Identity-based encryption using pairing-friendly curves for key exchange.

tldr.problem: Traditional public key encryption requires exchanging certificates or public keys before sending secrets. This is cumbersome when you want to send messages to recipients you haven't coordinated with beforehand.
tldr.mechanism: Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE) uses identity-based encryption (IBE), where the recipient's name or identifier can serve as a public key, derived using bilinear pairings on elliptic curves. A trusted key management service (KMS) provides private keys to authorized recipients.
tldr.outcome: A sender can securely transmit a shared secret to a receiver using only the receiver's identifier, without exchanging public keys in advance. This simplifies key distribution but requires a trusted KMS infrastructure.

facts.label: Security parameter
facts.value: lg(q) > 2n (where q is prime order, n is symmetric key size)

today: RFC 6508 is an Informational specification describing SAKKE for identity-based encryption. It has not been obsoleted and remains the reference for implementing this IBE scheme using pairing-friendly curves. SAKKE is used in some secure messaging and group communication protocols, but its adoption is limited compared to traditional public key infrastructure.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC describes the Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption (SAKKE) algorithm, an efficient implementation of identity-based encryption (IBE) using bilinear pairings on elliptic curves. With SAKKE, the receiver's identifier (such as a name or email) directly serves as their public key, eliminating the need to exchange public keys or certificates before secret transmission.

A trusted Key Management Service (KMS) generates a master secret and derives private keys for each enrolled user. When a sender wants to transmit a secret to a receiver, they use the receiver's identifier and the KMS's public parameters to encrypt it, and the receiver decrypts it using their private key.

This approach is especially useful in scenarios where you want to send secrets to recipients who may not yet be enrolled, as long as a KMS can assign them an identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine names are magic locks. The KMS gives each person a magic key for their name. Anyone who knows your name can use that name as a lock to send you a secret, and your magic key opens it.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
SAKKE is built on three foundational ideas. First, elliptic curve arithmetic: mathematical operations on points of an elliptic curve defined over a finite field. The specific curves used in SAKKE are supersingular curves chosen for computational efficiency. Second, bilinear pairings: a special function that takes two points on an elliptic curve and produces an element in another mathematical group. Third, identity-based public keys: instead of a random public key, the sender derives the encryption key from the receiver's identifier and public parameters provided by the KMS.

The KMS holds a Master Secret (z_T), a large random integer known only to the KMS. From this, the KMS computes its KMS Public Key (Z_T = [z_T]P), a curve point that is published and used by senders. For each user with identifier 'a', the KMS derives that user's Receiver Secret Key (RSK): K_(a,T) = [(a + z_T)^-1]P, a curve point that the user keeps private.
sections.plainLanguage: The KMS picks a big secret number. From that, it makes a public number everyone can see. Then for each person's name, it creates a private key by mixing the name with the secret in a special mathematical way.

sections.title: Key Exchange Process
sections.content:
SAKKE defines a two-step process: encapsulation by the sender and decapsulation by the receiver. A sender who wants to transmit a Shared Secret Value (SSV) to a receiver performs these steps: compute a value from the receiver's identifier, the public parameters, and the KMS's public key using the pairing; represent this value as a 128-bit (or n-bit) shared secret. The result is Encapsulated Data, consisting of a curve point and the encrypted shared secret value, which the sender transmits to the receiver.

The receiver who holds the Receiver Secret Key (RSK) decapsulates the data by computing the pairing using their private key and the curve point from the encapsulated data, recovering the same shared secret value. Once both sender and receiver share this secret, they can use it as a key for symmetric encryption to protect subsequent messages.

Importantly, the pairing computation is deterministic: given the same inputs, sender and receiver derive the same shared secret without further communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses the receiver's name and a public number to do a magic math trick, creating a locked box with a secret inside. The receiver uses their private key to do the same magic math trick and get the same secret out of the box, without the sender ever sending it directly.

sections.title: Mathematical Representation
sections.content:
SAKKE relies on specific mathematical structures. The elliptic curve E used is a supersingular curve with equation y² = x³ - 3x modulo a prime p. This particular curve form (choosing -3 for the coefficient) provides computational advantages in elliptic curve point arithmetic and allows efficient pairing computation.

The curve has a subgroup of order q, a large odd prime. A generator point P of this subgroup is published as part of the public parameters. The Tate-Lichtenbaum pairing is the specific bilinear pairing function used: it takes two points from the curve and produces an element in the multiplicative group. The RFC includes detailed pseudocode for computing this pairing using Miller's algorithm, with optimizations such as Barreto's trick to avoid expensive extension field computations.

All values—integers, field elements, curve points, and encapsulated data—have canonical octet string representations defined in the RFC to ensure interoperability across implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The math uses special curves and magic functions that work fast. The details are in the RFC so all programmers use the same curve and the same calculation method, so everyone gets compatible results.

sections.title: Practical Use and Security
sections.content:
SAKKE is suitable for scenarios where senders need to transmit secrets to multiple recipients identified by name or address, such as in group communications or broadcast secure messaging. It can be used alongside a single KMS shared by all parties, or with multiple KMSs if they agree on common public parameters.

The security of SAKKE depends on the hardness of the bilinear Diffie-Hellman problem on the chosen elliptic curve and the security of the chosen hash function. The RFC specifies parameter sizes to achieve different security levels: for n-bit symmetric key strength, the prime order q must have bit length greater than 2n to resist known attacks.

A critical requirement is that the KMS and its master secret remain secure. Compromise of the master secret allows an attacker to derive any user's private key. All parameters (p, q, E, P, g, hash function, and n) must be either application-specific constants or agreed upon through secure negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The system is safe as long as the KMS keeps its secret. Everyone uses the same curve and settings. If the KMS secret leaks, an attacker can make keys for anyone, so the KMS has to be carefully protected.
